recipe.history:
Okra — Abelmoschus esculentus — is one of the great vegetables of the African diaspora, a plant with origins in the highlands of Ethiopia and the savannahs of West Africa that traveled across the Atlantic in the hands and memories of enslaved Africans and became a cornerstone of the cuisines of the American South, the Caribbean, and Brazil. The plant's seed pods contain a mucilaginous substance that thickens soups and stews, a property that made it indispensable in gumbo — a dish whose very name derives from ki ngombo, the Bantu word for okra. In West Africa, okra has been used for centuries in stews with palm oil and chili peppers; in Egypt and the Middle East, it appears in tomato-based braises; in India, bhindi — fried or spiced okra — is a beloved side dish with its own regional traditions stretching across the subcontinent. The vegetable has been somewhat undervalued in mainstream American cooking outside the South, partly due to its mucilage, which can seem off-putting to cooks unfamiliar with it, but which disappears almost entirely when okra is cooked quickly at high heat or fried crisp.

In Southern American cooking, fried okra is a ritual and a pleasure — cornmeal-crusted, deep-fried until crackling and golden, salted heavily, and eaten immediately while the crust is still shattering. The tradition of frying okra to crisp it rather than stewing it to thicken soups is a testament to the culinary intelligence that recognized okra's transformative potential under high heat. On a burger, crispy fried okra does what the best burger toppings always do: it adds a completely different texture register to the assembly, the crunch of the cornmeal crust and the tender interior of the okra providing contrast against the yielding softness of the bun, the melted cheese, and the juicy patty. The flavor of fried okra — slightly vegetal, nutty from the cornmeal, savory from the frying oil — also complements beef beautifully, adding an earthy Southern richness that can't be replicated with any other ingredient.

I ate my first plate of truly excellent fried okra at a church supper in Alabama where someone's grandmother had made enough to feed approximately three times the number of people present, which is how church suppers work and why they are among the great institutions of American food culture. The okra was cut into rounds, dredged in seasoned cornmeal, and fried in a cast iron skillet that I am certain had not been washed with soap since the Carter administration. It came out of the oil golden and crackling, piled onto paper towels, salted immediately, and then disappearing from the platter at a rate that suggested everyone else in that church hall felt the same way I did. I put some on my plate with a piece of cornbread and stood there eating it and feeling very lucky to be in that room.

Crispy fried okra on a burger patty cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is a combination built on contrast. The okra brings crunch; the patty brings juice. The cornmeal coating is dry and savory; the medium-rare beef interior is wet and fatty. The textures and moisture levels are in constant, productive opposition, each bite delivering a different ratio of crunch to yield, crispness to juice. This tension is only possible when the patty is cooked to medium rare. Well-done beef, dried out and compressed, cannot provide the juicy counterweight that the crispy okra needs. The okra would dominate, the burger would taste like a vehicle for the topping rather than a collaboration between equals. Medium rare is the temperature at which the patty asserts itself and the fried okra finds a worthy partner.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
225g fresh okra pods, trimmed and sliced into 1/2-inch rounds
neutral oil for frying (enough for 2 inches depth)
1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
4 slices American cheese or mild cheddar
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and sprinkle sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.
6. Make the remoulade: Stir together mayonnaise, whole-grain Dijon, hot sauce, lemon juice, horseradish, Worcestershire, parsley, scallion, cayenne, and salt. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Fry the okra: Whisk buttermilk and egg together in a bowl. In a separate shallow bowl, combine cornmeal, flour, salt, garlic powder, onion powder, smoked paprika, cayenne, and black pepper. Toss okra rounds in the buttermilk mixture, then dredge thoroughly in the cornmeal mixture, pressing to adhere. Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or cast iron skillet to 350°F (175°C). Fry okra in batches, without crowding, for 2 to 3 minutes until deep golden and crispy. Drain on a wire rack over paper towels. Salt immediately. Keep warm.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and cayenne immediately before cooking.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
10. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Top each with a slice of cheese immediately.
11. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
13. Assemble: Spread remoulade generously on both cut faces of each bun.
14. Layer shredded lettuce, tomato slices, and red onion on the bottom bun.
15. Set the medium-rare cheese-topped patty on top.
16. Pile a generous heap of crispy fried okra rounds directly on top of the patty. The okra should be mounded high — this is not the time for restraint.
17. Cap with the top bun immediately, before the okra loses its crunch. Serve at once.
